logic_model.program_name: Keystone Family Housing: Rapid Rehousing, Stay Housed, and Fresh Start Furniture
logic_model.theory_of_change: If Keystone helps families move quickly into permanent housing with time-limited rent assistance, move-in essentials, and voluntary, individualized case management, then families can settle into housing and address barriers that threaten stability. This support is intended to help families remain housed after assistance ends, though housing stability also depends on factors outside Keystone’s control.
inputs: Executive director, four case managers, housing locator, and part-time finance manager
Rental assistance and program operating funds
About 20 volunteers and donated furniture
Small office and regional homeless response system
Referrals through regional coordinated entry
activities: Identify apartments and help families move into permanent housing
Pay security deposits and first month’s rent, then step down rent help for up to 12 months
Offer voluntary, individualized Stay Housed case management through home visits; frequency is adjusted with each family, with more frequent visits early when appropriate
Help families address budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care, and school enrollment based on their priorities
Provide Fresh Start Furniture move-in support by furnishing apartments before move-in
outputs: Families moved into permanent housing and days from enrollment to move-in
Rental assistance payments and duration of assistance
short_term_outcomes: Families move from homelessness into permanent housing
Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue
Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed
Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected
long_term_outcomes: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends
Fewer families return to homelessness or shelter
assumptions: Families can access suitable, affordable apartments in the local housing market
Families can choose whether to engage in case management and identify supports that fit their needs
Rent assistance, practical move-in support, and case management can address different barriers to housing stability
external_factors: Availability and affordability of rental housing
Changes in household income, employment, and benefit access
Availability of child care, school supports, and other community resources

measurement_plan.summary: This plan pairs existing program/HMIS records with a brief, voluntary participant check-in to track housing move-in, families’ confidence, stress, and resource knowledge. It also checks families’ housing status 12 months after move-in, where follow-up is feasible; results are reported as outcomes Keystone contributes to, not outcomes it alone causes. The participant survey has four recommended questions, below the requested limit of about eight.

metrics.name: Permanent-housing move-in and time to move-in
metrics.outcome: Families move from homelessness into permanent housing

questions.text: How many families in the reporting cohort have had the full, comparable observation period to move into housing?
questions.note: Use a consistent cohort definition and observation window, set to match applicable HMIS and award rules; show families not yet observed for the full period separately.

questions.text: How many families in that cohort moved into permanent housing during the observation period?
questions.note: Use the applicable HMIS/award definition for permanent-housing destination and move-in date.

questions.text: Among families who moved in, what was the median number of days from enrollment to move-in?
questions.note: Calculate from enrollment and physical move-in dates for the same cohort and observation period.

metrics.timing: Update enrollment and move-in records as they occur; review by reporting period using a consistent cohort and observation window. Separately show households not yet observed for the full window.
metrics.how_scored: Report the count and share of families in the fully observed cohort who moved into permanent housing, plus median days from enrollment to move-in among those who moved in. Show the cohort size and the not-yet-fully-observed count; align definitions with applicable HMIS and award rules.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are moving from homelessness into permanent housing and how quickly, a central rapid rehousing result.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC materials frame exits to permanent housing and time homeless as system performance indicators; Connecticut RRH describes helping households move into housing. These are useful alignment points, not automatically the project's required calculation. Confirm award-specific definitions. [S2, S17, S18, S19]

metrics.name: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
metrics.outcome: Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue

questions.text: Think about this same situation each time: you have a problem paying rent or with your landlord. How confident are you that you can take one next step to address it?
questions.note: Ask everyone about the same hypothetical situation at both survey points, whether or not they have a current issue. 0 = not at all confident; 10 = completely confident. Locally adapted check-in, not the validated housing self-efficacy scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you would know what to do if your landlord did not respond to a concern?
questions.note: Optional alternative; use the same hypothetical situation and 0–10 anchors at both survey points. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you could find someone or an organization to help with a rent or landlord issue?
questions.note: Optional alternative; overlaps somewhat with the separate resource-knowledge item. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at a consistent later point, such as program exit or the end of case-management support. Ask the same hypothetical scenario and item both times, after urgent intake needs are addressed.
metrics.how_scored: Report the item’s score distribution and median change for participants with paired answers, alongside baseline, follow-up, paired-response, and missing counts. Do not use a 1-point improvement threshold as a validated measure of meaningful change.
metrics.why_it_matters: A change in confidence can show whether families feel more able to take a next step when a housing problem arises.
metrics.funder_relevance: Housing-specific self-efficacy has been studied with people who are homeless or vulnerably housed. This brief locally adapted question adds a family-level view of a support outcome; it does not replace housing-status reporting. [S20]

metrics.name: Parent-reported stress
metrics.outcome: Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel that problems were too much to handle?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Response options: Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Very often. Do not combine a subset into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel worried about things you could not control?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Use the same five response options; do not combine items into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel you had enough support to manage your worries?
questions.note: Optional locally written item; higher frequency may indicate more support, not necessarily less stress. Do not combine it with the other items as a validated score.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items; use the same past-month time frame and response choices.
metrics.how_scored: Report responses to each item separately, with paired-response and missing counts. Lower frequency on the two included stress items suggests improvement. These are locally written items, not a validated scale; do not calculate a PSS-10 score. Confirm permission terms before reproducing or adapting any PSS-10 wording.
metrics.why_it_matters: Offers a brief view of parents’ reported stress while families work through housing-related challenges.
metrics.funder_relevance: The Community Foundation for Greater New Haven describes dignity and well-being as relevant to basic-needs work; this is a supplementary family-well-being measure, not a stated required metric. The PSS references inform the stress topic only; these items are not PSS-10 items. [S8, S21, S22]

metrics.name: Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need
metrics.outcome: Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know who you could contact?
questions.note: Offer Yes or No; participants may skip instead of answering. Keep the need broad and do not record personal details. At each survey point, record only its broad category where possible.

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know one place you could go for help?
questions.note: Optional alternative with the same broad-need and privacy guidance; locally adapted, not a validated test.

questions.text: Would you like help finding someone to contact about the need you chose?
questions.note: Optional service-planning alternative, not itself a measure of the outcome.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items. Compare answers over time only when the same broad need category is being discussed; if it changed or is unknown, report the answers separately rather than as a direct change.
metrics.how_scored: Report Yes, No, skipped, and missing responses separately. For paired comparisons, include only participants whose broad need category stayed the same. Record whether resource information was offered or accessed only if this can be done without personal details.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether parents feel they know where to turn for help with a priority they chose, consistent with individualized case management.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD housing-search and case-management resources include assessment and mainstream-resource referral tools, and 211 Connecticut provides housing and human-service referral information. This is a practical local check, not a stated funder requirement. [S23, S24]

metrics.name: Housing status 12 months after move-in
metrics.outcome: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends

questions.text: How many families are due for a 12-month housing-status follow-up after move-in?
questions.note: Set each family’s follow-up due date from the recorded physical move-in date. Use a consistent follow-up window. A 6-month check may also be collected where feasible, but the 12-month check is the priority.

questions.text: How many families due for follow-up were contacted, and how many had a known housing status?
questions.note: Keep contacted and known-status counts separate in the record. Use a consent-based, preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts; no impact on services. HMIS may not capture homelessness outside its system.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in permanent housing at follow-up?
questions.note: Count a move to another permanent unit as permanent housing; use consistent definitions at each follow-up window.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were staying in shelter, outside, or another place not meant for housing?
questions.note: Record the status source and follow-up date. Self-report supplements but is not equivalent to HUD’s HMIS-based system return-to-homelessness measure.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in another or unstable housing situation?
questions.note: Use a consistent local status definition; keep this category separate from permanent housing, homelessness, and unknown status.

metrics.timing: Prioritize a follow-up 12 months after each family’s recorded physical move-in date; collect a 6-month status after move-in too only where feasible. Use HMIS or a consent-based, brief follow-up with the family’s preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts. Do not imply every family can be reached.
metrics.how_scored: For each follow-up window, report the number due, contacted, with known status, and with unknown status. Among families with known status, report permanent housing, homelessness, and other/unstable housing separately; include the numerator and denominator for the share housed. Also show the number in permanent housing out of all families due, clearly labeled as including unknowns in the denominator. Unknown status is not evidence of either retention or housing loss. Treat any self-reported return as supplementary to, not equivalent to, the HMIS-based system measure; this is a contribution measure, not proof of program-caused retention.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are in permanent housing 12 months after move-in while making follow-up coverage and unknown status visible. This is a useful check on housing stability, though it may not always fall after rental assistance ends.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC system performance materials track permanent-housing exits and returns to homelessness; Connecticut RRH guidance provides the program context. A local 12-month follow-up from move-in is a practical measure, not an asserted state requirement, and self-report does not replace HMIS system reporting. [S6, S18, S25, S26]

tools.name: Brief participant check-in
tools.when: Offer at entry and at a consistent later point, after urgent intake needs are addressed. Use a short script: taking part is voluntary, any question may be skipped, and answers will not affect services. Offer read-aloud and translated options where available; use the same wording and response choices each time. The four included questions cover confidence, stress, and resource knowledge; optional items remain off unless Keystone chooses to add them.

Parent-reported stress
Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need

tools.name: Housing outcomes and follow-up records
tools.when: Use program records/HMIS throughout enrollment and move-in, with consistent cohort definitions and observation windows. Prioritize 12-month status after physical move-in; use a consent-based preferred contact method, limited attempts, and report due, contacted, known, and unknown status separately.

brand.standards: Keystone's look is warm, steady, and hopeful: never clinical, never pity-driven. Deep teal is our anchor color, with warm gold for highlights and a soft cream accent. Generous white space, rounded and friendly but not childish. Headlines in Georgia, body in Calibri. Show homes, keys, and neighborhoods, not people's faces. Always say 'families', never 'clients' or 'the homeless'.

questions.question: When you say a family has “kept their home,” how long after rental assistance ends do you mean, and what would you use to confirm the family is still housed?
questions.why: This makes Keystone’s central long-term outcome precise and helps us build a realistic way to measure it.
questions.answer: We enter everything required into the regional homeless data system: enrollments, exits to permanent housing, and how long families were homeless. Case managers log home visits. Honestly we rarely look at our own data beyond the required reports. The board keeps asking whether families are still housed a year after the rent help ends, and whether case management matters beyond the money. We do not have a good answer.

questions.question: During case management, what changes do you hope families make that help them stay housed, and what could staff realistically notice or record during visits?
questions.why: This helps clarify how case management may support housing stability and which changes can be tracked without creating an unrealistic burden.
questions.answer: In the first months families move in fast, usually within 45 days of enrolling, and kids get back into one school. Parents get calmer and start planning instead of reacting. They learn to budget around rent and know who to call when something goes wrong. A year out, what we hope for is that they are still housed, have not gone back to shelter, and have steadier income. Many parents tell us the biggest change is feeling in control again.

questions.why: This will help describe the program’s activities and the amount of support families receive.
questions.answer: We serve families with children who are living in shelter or doubled up, referred through the regional coordinated entry system. Most heads of household are single mothers in their twenties and thirties with one to three young kids. Many lost housing after an eviction, a job loss, or leaving a violent relationship. About a third speak Spanish at home. We serve roughly 70 families a year, about 220 people.

Third, Fresh Start Furniture: volunteers furnish the apartment before move-in day so families walk into a real home.

transcript.text: Thank you for sharing Keystone’s profile. I understand that you help families move from shelter into homes through apartment search, short-term rental assistance, home-based case management, and move-in furniture support. You already track key HMIS information and home visits, and you’re looking for a clearer picture of whether families stay housed and what difference the support makes.
Question 1 of 5: When you say a family has “kept their home,” how long after rental assistance ends do you mean, and what would you use to confirm the family is still housed?

We enter everything required into the regional homeless data system: enrollments, exits to permanent housing, and how long families were homeless. Case managers log home visits. Honestly we rarely look at our own data beyond the required reports. The board keeps asking whether families are still housed a year after the rent help ends, and whether case management matters beyond the money. We do not have a good answer.

You already record enrollments, exits to permanent housing, and homelessness length in the regional data system, and case managers log home visits. You’re not yet using those records to answer the board’s questions about housing stability one year later or what case management adds beyond rental assistance.
Question 2 of 5: During case management, what changes do you hope families make that help them stay housed, and what could staff realistically notice or record during visits?

In the first months families move in fast, usually within 45 days of enrolling, and kids get back into one school. Parents get calmer and start planning instead of reacting. They learn to budget around rent and know who to call when something goes wrong. A year out, what we hope for is that they are still housed, have not gone back to shelter, and have steadier income. Many parents tell us the biggest change is feeling in control again.

You hope families move into housing quickly, reconnect their children with one school, and build calmer, more practical ways to manage rent and problems. Longer term, success means staying housed, avoiding a return to shelter, and having steadier income; parents also describe feeling more in control.
Question 3 of 5: What does case management look like in practice—what support do families receive, how often do you meet or visit, and for how long?

We serve families with children who are living in shelter or doubled up, referred through the regional coordinated entry system. Most heads of household are single mothers in their twenties and thirties with one to three young kids. Many lost housing after an eviction, a job loss, or leaving a violent relationship. About a third speak Spanish at home. We serve roughly 70 families a year, about 220 people.

Thank you—that helps clarify who you serve: families with children living in shelter or doubled up, referred through coordinated entry, with about 70 families served each year. Many are navigating a recent housing loss, and about a third speak Spanish at home.
Question 4 of 5: What kinds of support do case managers typically provide to a family, and how often and for how long do they meet or visit?

Three things. First, rapid rehousing: our housing locator finds an apartment, we pay the security deposit and first month, then step rent help down over up to 12 months. Second, Stay Housed case management: weekly home visits for six months, then monthly, covering budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care and school enrollment. Third, Fresh Start Furniture: volunteers furnish the apartment before move-in day so families walk into a real home.

I’m hearing three connected pieces: help finding and moving into an apartment with rent support that steps down for up to 12 months, Stay Housed visits that shift from weekly to monthly, and volunteer-furnished homes before move-in. The visits cover practical needs like budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care, and school enrollment.
Question 5 of 5: Which grants or contracts fund these services, and what outcomes or reports do those funders ask you to provide?

About 55% of our money is federal homelessness funding passed through the regional Continuum of Care, 20% is state housing funds, 15% comes from local foundations and 10% from individual and congregational donors. The federal and state funders want exits to permanent housing and returns to homelessness. Foundations increasingly ask about family well-being and stories, not just placements.
Thank you, that's all five questions. Your team is now drafting your logic model.

Here is the revised logic model, with the housing pathway at its center and case management described as voluntary and tailored to each family. I removed income, calm/control, and school-continuity claims that were less directly supported, and made the near-term family changes more observable. Please edit any line directly or tell me what you’d like changed.

This is close. Please add our Fresh Start Furniture move-in support as its own activity, and make one short-term outcome about parents feeling more in control and less stressed, because families tell us that matters most.

I added Fresh Start Furniture as a clearly named move-in support activity and included the change families have emphasized: parents feeling more in control and less stressed. I kept the rest of the model as it was and retained alignment with common rapid-rehousing and housing-stability priorities. Please let me know if you’d like either new line worded differently.
Your logic model is approved. Next, let's choose how you'll know it's working.

Here is the revised measurement plan, with the team’s suggestions folded in. It keeps the participant check-in brief and voluntary, makes housing follow-up more feasible, and reports missing or unknown information openly. You can switch optional questions on or off, edit any wording, or tell me what you would like changed.
Please keep the participant survey short, no more than about 8 recommended questions, and make sure we measure whether families stay housed 12 months after move-in.

I’ve kept the participant survey to four recommended questions, with the optional alternatives still switched off. I also changed the housing follow-up to be measured 12 months after each family’s move-in date and made unknown status visible rather than treating it as housed or unhoused. One distinction to note: this follow-up may happen while rental assistance is still active for some families, so it complements—but does not replace—the outcome about staying housed after assistance ends.

approved_logic_model.program_name: Keystone Family Housing: Rapid Rehousing, Stay Housed, and Fresh Start Furniture
approved_logic_model.theory_of_change: If Keystone helps families move quickly into permanent housing with time-limited rent assistance, move-in essentials, and voluntary, individualized case management, then families can settle into housing and address barriers that threaten stability. This support is intended to help families remain housed after assistance ends, though housing stability also depends on factors outside Keystone’s control.
inputs: Executive director, four case managers, housing locator, and part-time finance manager
Rental assistance and program operating funds
About 20 volunteers and donated furniture
Small office and regional homeless response system
Referrals through regional coordinated entry
activities: Identify apartments and help families move into permanent housing
Pay security deposits and first month’s rent, then step down rent help for up to 12 months
Offer voluntary, individualized Stay Housed case management through home visits; frequency is adjusted with each family, with more frequent visits early when appropriate
Help families address budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care, and school enrollment based on their priorities
Provide Fresh Start Furniture move-in support by furnishing apartments before move-in
outputs: Families moved into permanent housing and days from enrollment to move-in
Rental assistance payments and duration of assistance

Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue
Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed
Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected
long_term_outcomes: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends
Fewer families return to homelessness or shelter
assumptions: Families can access suitable, affordable apartments in the local housing market
Families can choose whether to engage in case management and identify supports that fit their needs
Rent assistance, practical move-in support, and case management can address different barriers to housing stability
external_factors: Availability and affordability of rental housing

Availability of child care, school supports, and other community resources

plan.summary: This plan pairs existing program/HMIS records with a brief, voluntary participant check-in to track housing move-in, families’ confidence, stress, and resource knowledge. It also checks housing status after rental help ends where follow-up is feasible; results are reported as outcomes Keystone contributes to, not outcomes it alone causes.

metrics.name: Permanent-housing move-in and time to move-in
metrics.outcome: Families move from homelessness into permanent housing

questions.text: How many families in the reporting cohort have had the full, comparable observation period to move into housing?
questions.note: Use a consistent cohort definition and observation window, set to match applicable HMIS and award rules; show families not yet observed for the full period separately.

questions.text: How many families in that cohort moved into permanent housing during the observation period?
questions.note: Use the applicable HMIS/award definition for permanent-housing destination and move-in date.

questions.text: Among families who moved in, what was the median number of days from enrollment to move-in?
questions.note: Calculate from enrollment and physical move-in dates for the same cohort and observation period.

metrics.timing: Update enrollment and move-in records as they occur; review by reporting period using a consistent cohort and observation window. Separately show households not yet observed for the full window.
metrics.how_scored: Report the count and share of families in the fully observed cohort who moved into permanent housing, plus median days from enrollment to move-in among those who moved in. Show the cohort size and the not-yet-fully-observed count; align definitions with applicable HMIS and award rules.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are moving from homelessness into permanent housing and how quickly, a central rapid rehousing result.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC materials frame exits to permanent housing and time homeless as system performance indicators; Connecticut RRH describes helping households move into housing. These are useful alignment points, not automatically the project's required calculation. Confirm award-specific definitions. [S2, S17, S18, S19]

metrics.name: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
metrics.outcome: Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue

questions.text: Think about this same situation each time: you have a problem paying rent or with your landlord. How confident are you that you can take one next step to address it?
questions.note: Ask everyone about the same hypothetical situation at both survey points, whether or not they have a current issue. 0 = not at all confident; 10 = completely confident. Locally adapted check-in, not the validated housing self-efficacy scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you would know what to do if your landlord did not respond to a concern?
questions.note: Optional alternative; use the same hypothetical situation and 0–10 anchors at both survey points. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you could find someone or an organization to help with a rent or landlord issue?
questions.note: Optional alternative; overlaps somewhat with the separate resource-knowledge item. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at a consistent later point, such as program exit or the end of case-management support. Ask the same hypothetical scenario and item both times, after urgent intake needs are addressed.
metrics.how_scored: Report the item’s score distribution and median change for participants with paired answers, alongside baseline, follow-up, paired-response, and missing counts. Do not use a 1-point improvement threshold as a validated measure of meaningful change.
metrics.why_it_matters: A change in confidence can show whether families feel more able to take a next step when a housing problem arises.
metrics.funder_relevance: Housing-specific self-efficacy has been studied with people who are homeless or vulnerably housed. This brief locally adapted question adds a family-level view of a support outcome; it does not replace housing-status reporting. [S20]

metrics.name: Parent-reported stress
metrics.outcome: Parents report feeling more in control and less stressed

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel that problems were too much to handle?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Response options: Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Very often. Do not combine a subset into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel worried about things you could not control?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Use the same five response options; do not combine items into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel you had enough support to manage your worries?
questions.note: Optional locally written item; higher frequency may indicate more support, not necessarily less stress. Do not combine it with the other items as a validated score.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items; use the same past-month time frame and response choices.
metrics.how_scored: Report responses to each item separately, with paired-response and missing counts. Lower frequency on the two included stress items suggests improvement. These are locally written items, not a validated scale; do not calculate a PSS-10 score. Confirm permission terms before reproducing or adapting any PSS-10 wording.
metrics.why_it_matters: Offers a brief view of parents’ reported stress while families work through housing-related challenges.
metrics.funder_relevance: The Community Foundation for Greater New Haven describes dignity and well-being as relevant to basic-needs work; this is a supplementary family-well-being measure, not a stated required metric. The PSS references inform the stress topic only; these items are not PSS-10 items. [S8, S21, S22]

metrics.name: Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need
metrics.outcome: Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know who you could contact?
questions.note: Offer Yes or No; participants may skip instead of answering. Keep the need broad and do not record personal details. At each survey point, record only its broad category where possible.

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know one place you could go for help?
questions.note: Optional alternative with the same broad-need and privacy guidance; locally adapted, not a validated test.

questions.text: Would you like help finding someone to contact about the need you chose?
questions.note: Optional service-planning alternative, not itself a measure of the outcome.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items. Compare answers over time only when the same broad need category is being discussed; if it changed or is unknown, report the answers separately rather than as a direct change.
metrics.how_scored: Report Yes, No, skipped, and missing responses separately. For paired comparisons, include only participants whose broad need category stayed the same. Record whether resource information was offered or accessed only if this can be done without personal details.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether parents feel they know where to turn for help with a priority they chose, consistent with individualized case management.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD housing-search and case-management resources include assessment and mainstream-resource referral tools, and 211 Connecticut provides housing and human-service referral information. This is a practical local check, not a stated funder requirement. [S23, S24]

metrics.name: Housing retention after rental assistance ends
metrics.outcome: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends

questions.text: How many families are due for a 12-month housing-status follow-up after rental assistance ends?
questions.note: Make 12-month status the priority if staff capacity is limited; report 6-month results only where feasible.

questions.text: How many families due for follow-up were contacted, and how many had a known housing status?
questions.note: Keep contacted and known-status counts separate in the record. Use a consent-based, preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts; no impact on services. HMIS may not capture homelessness outside its system.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in permanent housing at follow-up?
questions.note: Count a move to another permanent unit as permanent housing; use consistent definitions at each follow-up window.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were staying in shelter, outside, or another place not meant for housing?
questions.note: Record the status source and follow-up date. Self-report supplements but is not equivalent to HUD’s HMIS-based system return-to-homelessness measure.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in another or unstable housing situation?
questions.note: Use a consistent local status definition; keep this category separate from permanent housing, homelessness, and unknown status.

metrics.timing: Prioritize 12 months after rental assistance ends; collect 6-month status too only where feasible. Use HMIS or a consent-based, brief follow-up with the family’s preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts. Do not imply every family can be reached.
metrics.how_scored: For each follow-up window, report due, contacted, known-status, and unknown counts. Among known statuses, report permanent housing, homelessness, and other/unstable housing separately. Also show the number in permanent housing out of all families due, clearly labeled as including unknowns in the denominator. Treat any self-reported return as supplementary to, not equivalent to, the HMIS-based system measure; this is a contribution measure, not proof of program-caused retention.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families remain in permanent housing after rent assistance ends while making follow-up coverage and unknown status visible.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC system performance materials track permanent-housing exits and returns to homelessness; Connecticut RRH guidance provides the program context. Local 12-month follow-up is a practical measure, not an asserted state requirement, and self-report does not replace HMIS system reporting. [S6, S18, S25, S26]

tools.name: Brief participant check-in
tools.when: Offer at entry and at a consistent later point, after urgent intake needs are addressed. Use a short script: taking part is voluntary, any question may be skipped, and answers will not affect services. Offer read-aloud and translated options where available; use the same wording and response choices each time. The four included questions cover confidence, stress, and resource knowledge.
metrics: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
Parent-reported stress
Knowing where to seek help for a chosen need

tools.name: Housing outcomes and follow-up records
tools.when: Use program records/HMIS throughout enrollment and move-in, with consistent cohort definitions and observation windows. Prioritize 12-month status after assistance ends when feasible; use a consent-based preferred contact method, limited attempts, and report contacted, known, and unknown status separately.

These are useful alignment points, not automatically the project's required calculation. Confirm award-specific definitions. [S2, S17, S18, S19]

metrics.name: Confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue
metrics.outcome: Families report greater confidence taking a next step to address a rent or landlord issue

questions.text: Think about this same situation each time: you have a problem paying rent or with your landlord. How confident are you that you can take one next step to address it?
questions.note: Ask everyone about the same hypothetical situation at both survey points, whether or not they have a current issue. 0 = not at all confident; 10 = completely confident. Locally adapted check-in, not the validated housing self-efficacy scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you would know what to do if your landlord did not respond to a concern?
questions.note: Optional alternative; use the same hypothetical situation and 0–10 anchors at both survey points. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

questions.text: How confident are you that you could find someone or an organization to help with a rent or landlord issue?
questions.note: Optional alternative; overlaps somewhat with the separate resource-knowledge item. Locally adapted item, not a validated scale.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at a consistent later point, such as program exit or the end of case-management support. Ask the same hypothetical scenario and item both times, after urgent intake needs are addressed.
metrics.how_scored: Report the item’s score distribution and median change for participants with paired answers, alongside baseline, follow-up, paired-response, and missing counts. Do not use a 1-point improvement threshold as a validated measure of meaningful change.
metrics.why_it_matters: A change in confidence can show whether families feel more able to take a next step when a housing problem arises.
metrics.funder_relevance: Housing-specific self-efficacy has been studied with people who are homeless or vulnerably housed. This brief locally adapted question adds a family-level view of a support outcome; it does not replace housing-status reporting. [S20]

metrics.name: Parent-reported stress

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel that problems were too much to handle?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Response options: Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Often, Very often. Do not combine a subset into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel worried about things you could not control?
questions.note: Locally written check-in item, not copied from the PSS-10. Use the same five response options; do not combine items into a PSS-10 score.

questions.text: In the past month, how often did you feel you had enough support to manage your worries?
questions.note: Optional locally written item; higher frequency may indicate more support, not necessarily less stress. Do not combine it with the other items as a validated score.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items; use the same past-month time frame and response choices.
metrics.how_scored: Report responses to each item separately, with paired-response and missing counts. Lower frequency on the two included stress items suggests improvement. metrics.funder_relevance: The Community Foundation for Greater New Haven describes dignity and well-being as relevant to basic-needs work; this is a supplementary family-well-being measure, not a stated required metric. metrics.outcome: Parents can identify where to seek help for at least one priority need they selected

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know who you could contact?
questions.note: Offer Yes or No; participants may skip instead of answering. Keep the need broad and do not record personal details. At each survey point, record only its broad category where possible.

questions.text: If you wanted help with a need you chose, do you know one place you could go for help?

questions.text: Would you like help finding someone to contact about the need you chose?
questions.note: Optional service-planning alternative, not itself a measure of the outcome.

metrics.timing: At program entry and at the same later point used for the other check-in items. Compare answers over time only when the same broad need category is being discussed; if it changed or is unknown, report the answers separately rather than as a direct change.
metrics.how_scored: Report Yes, No, skipped, and missing responses separately. For paired comparisons, include only participants whose broad need category stayed the same. Record whether resource information was offered or accessed only if this can be done without personal details.
metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether parents feel they know where to turn for help with a priority they chose, consistent with individualized case management.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD housing-search and case-management resources include assessment and mainstream-resource referral tools, and 211 Connecticut provides housing and human-service referral information. This is a practical local check, not a stated funder requirement. [S23, S24]

metrics.name: Housing status 12 months after move-in
metrics.outcome: Families remain housed after time-limited rental assistance ends

questions.text: How many families are due for a 12-month housing-status follow-up after move-in?
questions.note: Set each family’s follow-up due date from the recorded physical move-in date. Use a consistent follow-up window. A 6-month check may also be collected where feasible, but the 12-month check is the priority.

questions.text: How many families due for follow-up were contacted, and how many had a known housing status?
questions.note: Keep contacted and known-status counts separate in the record. Use a consent-based, preferred contact method and a limited, pre-set number of attempts; no impact on services. HMIS may not capture homelessness outside its system.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in permanent housing at follow-up?
questions.note: Count a move to another permanent unit as permanent housing; use consistent definitions at each follow-up window.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were staying in shelter, outside, or another place not meant for housing?
questions.note: Record the status source and follow-up date. Self-report supplements but is not equivalent to HUD’s HMIS-based system return-to-homelessness measure.

questions.text: How many families with a known status were in another or unstable housing situation?
questions.note: Use a consistent local status definition; keep this category separate from permanent housing, homelessness, and unknown status.

metrics.timing: Prioritize a follow-up 12 months after each family’s recorded physical move-in date; collect a 6-month status after move-in too only where feasible. metrics.why_it_matters: Shows whether families are in permanent housing 12 months after move-in while making follow-up coverage and unknown status visible. This is a useful check on housing stability, though it may not always fall after rental assistance ends.
metrics.funder_relevance: HUD CoC system performance materials track permanent-housing exits and returns to homelessness; Connecticut RRH guidance provides the program context. A local 12-month follow-up from move-in is a practical measure, not an asserted state requirement, and self-report does not replace HMIS system reporting. [S6, S18, S25, S26]

request.notes: This is for our renewal conversation with a regional family foundation. Lead with housing stability, show who we serve, and close with the cost of keeping a family housed.

draft.deck_subtitle: Housing stability takes more than a move-in

slides.headline: A home to build on
body: Keystone Family Housing Partners
Funder renewal conversation
slides.speaker_notes: Thank you for making time to hear about Keystone Family Housing Partners. Our work starts with a practical goal: helping families move from homelessness into permanent housing, and helping them build the supports and confidence that can make a home more stable. We will share what the current participant feedback tells us, what it does not yet tell us, and where continued foundation support can help. Our guiding idea is simple: every family, a home to build on.

slides.headline: A move-in is a beginning
body: A lease starts housing stability; practical support helps families work toward keeping it.
slides.speaker_notes: A move into a home matters enormously, but it is not the whole story. Rent, landlord issues, benefits, child care, school enrollment, and the pressure of settling in can all affect whether a family feels able to move forward. Keystone’s approach pairs help getting into permanent housing with time-limited rent assistance, move-in essentials, and voluntary individualized support. That support is intended to help families remain housed after assistance ends, while recognizing that housing stability also depends on factors outside Keystone’s control.

slides.headline: Pair a home with practical support
body: Find an apartment and help families move in
Provide deposits, stepped-down rent help, and furniture
Offer voluntary, individualized case management
Support family-selected steps toward housing stability
slides.speaker_notes: The program combines several supports around each move. Keystone identifies apartments and helps families move into permanent housing, provides security deposits and first month’s rent, and steps down rental help for up to 12 months. Fresh Start Furniture furnishes apartments before move-in. Stay Housed case management is voluntary and individualized, with home-visit frequency adjusted with each family. Together, these supports are meant to ease the move and help families address the practical barriers they identify as important.

slides.headline: A promising signal from matched responses
slides.speaker_notes: The results here come from a small reporting group, so we want to be clear about who answered. There were 24 participants represented in the headline data, and 20 provided both a pre and post response. Among participants who answered both surveys, 85% improved in confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue. That is an encouraging participant-reported signal. It is not a claim that every family improved, and it is not by itself evidence of long-term housing stability.

slides.headline: More participants reported improvement
body: Among participants who answered both surveys, improvement was most common in confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue.
slides.speaker_notes: This chart brings together three participant-reported measures. Among people with both a pre and a post answer, 85% improved in confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue, 60% improved in knowing where to seek help for a chosen need, and 70% improved on the parent-reported stress measure. Improvement means at least one point higher on a rating scale, or a change from no to yes. These are meaningful short-term signals, but they describe reported change—not proof that the program alone caused it.

slides.headline: Confidence addressing housing issues rose
body: Participants who answered both surveys reported higher average confidence taking a next step on a rent or landlord issue.
slides.speaker_notes: For the confidence measure, the average rating was 3.35 before and 6.6 after, on a scale from 0 to 10. The same 20 participants answered both the pre and post surveys. This change is consistent with the program’s focus on helping families work through rent and landlord concerns. A confidence rating does not mean a problem was solved, or that a housing challenge will not arise. It does suggest that many respondents felt better equipped to take a next step.

slides.headline: More knew where to seek help
body: The share answering yes about where to seek help for a chosen need rose from 20% to 70%.
slides.speaker_notes: This measure asks whether parents know where to seek help for a priority need they chose. Among the 20 participants who answered both surveys, 20% said yes before and 70% said yes after. Knowing where to turn can be a useful step toward addressing needs such as benefits, child care, budgeting, or school enrollment, depending on the family’s priorities. This is a reported measure of knowing where to seek help; it does not tell us whether a service was available or whether the need was ultimately resolved.

slides.headline: Parents reported a better stress measure
body: The reverse-scored average moved from 2.55 to 3.6, where higher means better.
slides.speaker_notes: The stress measure is reverse-scored, so a higher number indicates a better result on this scale. The average moved from 2.55 before to 3.6 after among the 20 participants who answered both surveys. The chart offers a brief view of how parents reported stress while navigating housing-related challenges. It should be read as a change in survey responses, not as a clinical assessment or a promise that stress has gone away. Families’ experiences and circumstances can continue to change.

slides.headline: Follow-up tracking is still developing
body: By 2026-09, 11 families had the full comparable observation period for move-in tracking; this is not a move-in result.
slides.speaker_notes: This staff-entered indicator tracks how many families in the reporting cohort have had a full, comparable observation period to move into housing. The count is 11 in 2026-09. It helps us understand whether the cohort has had enough comparable time for move-in tracking; it does not tell us how many families moved into housing or remained housed. We include it because careful timing and follow-up matter when interpreting outcomes. We want to keep building reporting that separates program activity, move-in results, and longer-term stability.

slides.headline: Respondents were families with children
body: 100% of participants who answered reported children under 18 at home.
slides.speaker_notes: This profile chart shows that 100% of the 24 participants who answered reported children under 18 at home. It is one useful piece of context for understanding the families represented in these responses, not a complete description of every family Keystone serves. We are keeping this profile at an aggregate level and not presenting small demographic groups. The program’s work with families—from securing a home to arranging move-in essentials and individualized support—is grounded in the realities of family life.

slides.headline: Knowing who to call matters
slides.quote: It's still hard some months but I know who to call now.
slides.speaker_notes: This participant’s words hold both parts of the experience: some months are still hard, and knowing who to call is a change they value. We appreciate that the quote does not suggest that support removes every challenge. It speaks instead to one of the program’s intended short-term outcomes: helping parents identify where to seek help for a priority need. We share this anonymously, alongside the survey results, as one person’s perspective rather than as a summary of every family’s experience.

slides.headline: Encouraging signals, with important limits
body: Matched survey responses show reported short-term changes
The current results do not establish long-term housing stability
A 12-month housing-status result is not included here
Keep improving follow-up and cost reporting
slides.speaker_notes: The matched responses give us a useful view of short-term changes in confidence, knowing where to seek help, and reported stress. There are important limits: 20 participants answered both surveys, results are self-reported, and we cannot attribute every change to Keystone. The materials provided do not include a 12-month housing-status result, so we are not claiming that these data demonstrate that families remained housed after assistance ended. Better follow-up and clearer reporting on program costs would help the foundation and Keystone assess progress more fully.

slides.headline: Sustain the supports around a move
body: Renew support for time-limited rent assistance
Keep move-in essentials and voluntary case management available
Strengthen follow-up on housing status and program costs
slides.speaker_notes: For this renewal conversation, we are asking for support that helps sustain the combination of supports around a family’s move: time-limited rent assistance, move-in essentials through Fresh Start Furniture, and voluntary, individualized Stay Housed case management. We do not have a cost-per-family figure in the information we are sharing today, so we will not put forward an unsupported amount. Support can also help Keystone strengthen follow-up on housing status and cost reporting, so future renewal conversations can connect resources with clearer outcome information.

slides.headline: Thank you
body: Every family, a home to build on
keystonefamilyhousing.example.org
slides.speaker_notes: Thank you for considering Keystone’s work and for investing in families as they move toward a stable home. The participant responses shared today are encouraging, while also reminding us to keep listening and to improve how we track longer-term housing status and costs. We welcome a conversation about the mix of support that can help families settle into housing and address the barriers they identify. You can learn more or connect with Keystone at keystonefamilyhousing.example.org.

answers.question: Organization background
answers.answer:
Keystone Family Housing Partners works to help families move from homelessness into permanent housing and address barriers that can threaten housing stability. Through Keystone Family Housing: Rapid Rehousing, Stay Housed, and Fresh Start Furniture, we combine housing search and move-in assistance, time-limited rental support, voluntary individualized case management, and donated furniture. Case managers work with families on priorities such as budgeting, landlord issues, benefits, child care, and school enrollment. Our approach is grounded in the understanding that families’ housing stability also depends on circumstances beyond our control.

Our program draws on a housing locator, case-management and finance capacity, volunteers, donated furniture, and referrals through a regional homeless response system. Recent program records show {{total:active-landlord-partners}} active landlord partners during the reporting period, and volunteers furnished {{total:apartments-furnished-by-volunteers}} apartments. answers.question: Need
answers.answer:
Families experiencing homelessness need a path into permanent housing as well as practical support to address the challenges that can put a tenancy at risk. A move alone may not resolve landlord concerns, financial pressures, or families’ other priority needs. Keystone responds by helping families locate housing, cover move-in costs and rent for a limited period, and access voluntary case management tailored to their circumstances.

Our program records track movement into permanent housing for a comparable cohort: {{total:how-many-families-in-that-cohort-moved-into-perm}} of {{total:how-many-families-in-the-reporting-cohort-have-h}} families moved into permanent housing during the observation period. Among families with a known housing status at follow-up, {{total:how-many-families-with-a-known-status-were-in-pe}} were in permanent housing; we report known status separately because not every family’s housing status is necessarily known. Families’ own feedback also points to the value of support with housing and family stability. answers.question: Program description
answers.answer:
Keystone Family Housing combines rapid rehousing with voluntary, individualized support to help families move into housing and work toward stability. We identify apartments with families, help with security deposits and initial rent, and step down rental assistance over a limited period. Fresh Start Furniture provides move-in essentials before families settle into their apartments. Through Stay Housed, case managers make home visits at a frequency shaped with each family, with more frequent contact early when appropriate. Families choose the issues they want to address, which may include budgeting, landlord communication, benefits, child care, or school enrollment.

This approach is intended to help families settle into housing and build their ability to respond to challenges; it does not assume that Keystone alone determines whether a family remains housed. The program is supported by landlord relationships, volunteers, donated furnishings, and referrals through a regional homeless response system. During the reporting period, Keystone paid {{total:rental-assistance-paid-to-landlords}} in rental assistance to landlords and furnished {{total:apartments-furnished-by-volunteers}} apartments. answers.question: Outcomes and evaluation
answers.answer:
We measure both housing progress and families’ reported experience. Program records track move-ins and time from enrollment to move-in using a consistent cohort and observation window; we separately identify families who have not yet had the full observation period. In the latest reporting period, {{latest:how-many-families-in-that-cohort-moved-into-perm}} of {{latest:how-many-families-in-the-reporting-cohort-have-h}} families in the comparable cohort moved into permanent housing. We also follow up on housing status after move-in and report how many families were due for follow-up, contacted, and had a known status, rather than treating unknown status as a result.

We use the same participant check-in items at entry and a later point. Among {{matched}} participants who answered both surveys, {{improved:confidence-addressing-a-rent-or-landlord-issue}} improved on confidence addressing a rent or landlord issue, {{improved:knowing-where-to-seek-help-for-a-chosen-need}} improved on knowing where to seek help for a chosen need, and {{improved:parent-reported-stress}} improved on the parent-reported stress measure. These are reported changes, not proof that the program alone caused them. We will use program records and survey results to review progress and adjust delivery.
